text: NDMA: Stay well-hydrated; carry and drink plenty of clean water throughout the day. Avoid direct exposure to sunlight, especially during peak hours (11:00 AM to 4:00 PM).
NDMA: Plan outdoor work or physical activity during cooler parts of the day and avoid unnecessary travel.
NDMA: Give special attention to the elderly, infants and those with pre-existing health conditions. In case of symptoms like dizziness, nausea, or weakness, consult a doctor immediately.

NDMA: Use lightweight, loose-fitting and light-colored clothing, along with SPF and hats. Use curtains, shades or blinds to reduce indoor heat, and place fans near windows at night to improve ventilation.

WHO: Outdoor and manual workers, athletes, older adults, young children, people with chronic conditions and people living alone are at higher risk from heat; heatstroke is a medical emergency with a high case-fatality rate.

WHO: Avoid going outside and doing strenuous activity during the hottest time of day; drink water regularly; take cool showers or baths; check in with vulnerable people; never leave children or animals in parked vehicles.
US EPA AQI (2024 breakpoints): PM2.5 0.0-9.0 ug/m3 = Good (0-50); 9.1-35.4 = Moderate (51-100), when unusually sensitive people may be at risk.
US EPA AQI (2024 breakpoints): PM2.5 35.5-55.4 ug/m3 = Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups (101-150); 55.5-125.4 = Unhealthy (151-200), when the general public may experience health effects.
US EPA AQI (2024 breakpoints): PM2.5 125.5-225.4 ug/m3 = Very Unhealthy (201-300, health alert for everyone); 225.5 and above = Hazardous (301+).

NWS heat index: 80-90 F Caution (fatigue possible); 90-103 F Extreme Caution (heat stroke, cramps or exhaustion possible); 103-124 F Danger (cramps or exhaustion likely, heat stroke possible); 125 F or higher Extreme Danger (heat stroke highly likely).
